signals: only ever need to read tickets and draft replies
stem: A team exposes a customer-support agent that can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds, and delete user accounts. Support staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies.
ask: Applying least-privilege principles, which change best reduces risk?

options.text: Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited later.
options.why: Logging is a detective control: it tells you about misuse after the refund or deletion has happened, and leaves the unneeded privilege in place.

options.text: Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely.
options.why: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not require. With refund and delete gone, there is no attack surface left to monitor or guard.

options.text: Keep all tools but add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
options.why: A confirmation step is a compensating control. The agent still holds refund and delete, so a prompt injection or a mistaken approval can still use them.

options.text: Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.
options.why: Model size has nothing to do with authorization scope. A more obedient model still holds tools the role should never have.

explain: Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not require, eliminating the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it. Logging (A) and confirmations (C) are detective/compensating controls, not removal of unnecessary privilege; model size (D) is unrelated to authorization scope.

src.ref: Anthropic, Claude Certified Architect – Professional Exam Guide v1.0 (July 2026), Section 8, Sample 1

signals: same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request
Latency and cost are both concerns
stem: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost are both concerns.
ask: Which optimization most directly addresses both?

options.text: Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens.
options.why: Truncation discards policy the model needs, trading correctness for savings instead of reusing the stable prefix.

options.text: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit.
options.why: Downsizing regardless of task fit risks quality; it is a blunt cut that ignores whether the smaller model clears the bar.

options.text: Place the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching.
options.why: Stable content first plus prompt caching reuses the repeated prefix, cutting both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without losing context.

options.text: Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.
options.why: Relocating the policy into few-shot examples does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix; the same tokens are still resent and reprocessed.

explain: Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets repeated prefixes be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. Truncation (A) loses needed policy; downsizing blindly (B) risks quality; relocating to few-shot (D) does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix.

signals: latency and model version are unchanged
stem: A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged.
ask: What is the most likely first place to investigate?

options.text: The model weights have silently changed.
options.why: Model version is stated as unchanged, and nothing in a document refresh touches weights; blaming them ignores the variable that did change.

options.text: The retrieval/indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
options.why: The document refresh is the only change. Confident but wrong answers point to retrieval feeding poor context, such as a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings.

options.text: The temperature setting is too low.
options.why: A low temperature makes output more deterministic; it would not be triggered by a document refresh or explain newly wrong answers.
Nothing about a refresh shrinks the context window; the configured window is independent of the corpus contents.

explain: Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options would not be triggered specifically by a document refresh.
